transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-03-12
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62m
Location: Zoom / Lyric Systems - Redwood technical deep dive
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Sofia Ortega (Redwood SE), Connor Wu (Redwood Obs), Priya Nair (Lyric Platform), Gunnar Holt (Lyric SRE), Marta Rivera (Lyric CTO), Lee Tran (Lyric Infra)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Deep dive on tail latency sources observed in Lyric's staging cluster when traffic fans out to edge proxies and cross-vpc shards. Focus: streaming vs non-streaming paths, KV hotkeys, shard fanout thresholds, quantization side-effects at runtime.
- Agreed to exchange traces and run synthetic tests; plan on on-prem pilot.

Topics discussed:
- Observed p95/p99 spikes on bursts that correlate with KV shard rebalancing and edge proxy conntrack saturation
- Streaming vs batch: serialization overhead vs per-token overheads and effect on jitter
- Quantization: kernel variance and cold-cache deserialization penalty
- VPC egress and multi-nic routing adding 1-3 network hops in worst-case
- Autoscaling and shard-level throttles (fanout threshold)

Transcript body:
00:00 Avery Chen: all right thanks everyone for joining, uh we know Lyric has been seeing intermittent p99 jumps on the staging workload so today Marcus and I wanted to go knee deep into the runtime traces and the kv fanout pattern and uh dissect streaming vs batch behavior, sound good?
00:11 Priya Nair: yeah that's perfect, thanks. we shared the flamegraphs earlier, not sure if they made it through the recording but good to talk through them live
00:22 Marcus Lee: i pulled the trace for last friday's 2:05pm spike — you'll see a pattern where a single request fans out to 12 kv shards then a few of those stall, causing waterfall amplification, p99 is very sensitive to the slowest tail
00:38 Gunnar Holt: yes, exactly — when we had the short outage the egress tables showed 2 extra network hops for roughly 6% of connections, we thought it was mesh, maybe conntrack or iptables rules bouncing?
00:52 Marcus Lee: could be, we also see per-shard CPU jitter. when a shard hits hotkeys the kv backend falls back to single-threaded flush in your config, that matches the timeline
01:05 Marta Rivera: quick q — are we sure that's kv and not inference kernel cold-starts? our quantized model warms up at first generation and then stays steady
01:14 Sofia Ortega: good point, quantization can change kernel selection heuristics; some kernels have higher variance for short sequences, we saw that with our 8-bit fp8-ish path — not deterministic across devices
01:29 Lee Tran: we also have multi-nic routing on the edge pods, sometimes the packet crosses AZ boundary for HA routes which adds another 10-20ms; combined with a slow shard it's visible at p99
01:44 Avery Chen: right so there are at least three orthogonal contributors: network hop variance, kv fanout/hotkey stalls, and kernel variance from quantization/cold kv cache. let's walk snapshots.
02:00 Marcus Lee: (screen share) here's request 0x7a9 — you can see timeline: initial accept -> prefix cache miss -> kv fanout to 12 shards -> two shards returned after 8ms, one shard stalled at ~120ms because it hit the per-shard I/O stall due to internal flush. that stall dominoes
02:24 Priya Nair: that shard is on a node that had a backup job running; we didn't know the backup overlaps with the kv shard rebalancer, bad timing
02:34 Marcus Lee: yeah that would explain it — it's the classic interference. two mitigations here: either reduce shard fanout thresholds (so fewer shards per request) or enable streaming so partial tokens get returned while slow shards finish, but streaming has tradeoffs for your front-end because it changes token accounting and latencies per token
02:56 Gunnar Holt: when you say reduce fanout threshold do you mean at the request router level or in the kv config?
03:03 Marcus Lee: at the router/aggregator layer — set a soft cap on concurrent shard requests per inference call; if more shards would be invoked we do a best-effort merge or sequential fallback, that's what we call fanout-threshold.
03:15 Marta Rivera: what's the effect on QoR? we can't drop top-k fidelity for some of our safety pipelines.
03:23 Sofia Ortega: we usually recommend pinning critical safety checks to dedicated shards or using progressive result merging where we wait for top-N shards deterministically and fall back on a compacted representation for the rest. it's a small model-level change but reduces p99 dramatically
03:41 Lee Tran: about streaming — we ran it in staging and saw better median but p99 sometimes worsened because extra round trips to the edge increase exposure to network hop jitter
03:55 Marcus Lee: that's true. streaming reduces perceived latency for users because early tokens arrive sooner, but end-to-end p99 for a full-generation task can be higher if downstream acknowledgements are serialized across hops. so streaming helps UX for some flows but not all
04:18 Priya Nair: can we instrument per-hop time in tracing? our current traces show aggregate network time only
04:25 Connor Wu: yes we can add per-hop labels — we need to propagate trace IDs across the edge proxy and internal mesh, and instrument conntrack metrics. we'll add that to the telemetry plan
04:35 Gunnar Holt: does Redwood's runtime batcher change behavior when streaming is on? we saw batch sizes drop which increased per-token GPU overhead.
04:45 Marcus Lee: streaming disables some wait windows in the continuous batcher, so batch size reduces for short latency targets; that increases GPU per-token cost but reduces median latency. it's a cost/latency tradeoff
05:02 Marta Rivera: quantization then — we tried int8 surprisal path; noticed tail spikes when a hot shard rehydrates kv-cache and triggers unpacking on CPU which blocks the node for a few ms
05:17 Sofia Ortega: that's a known pattern — quantized checkpoints often have a short unpack/deserialization penalty on load which looks like a cold-cache problem. two mitigations: warm the checkpoints with a lightweight prefetch and adopt memory-mapped quant containers where supported
05:34 Priya Nair: how much does mmap help? we have a lot of ephemeral on-prem nodes so cold-start is common
05:40 Marcus Lee: mmap can drop that unpack window from 30-50ms to single-digit micro ops assuming the kernel is not swapping. but on heavy I/O contention it's still variable. for on-prem sometimes the filesystem is the bottleneck
05:53 Lee Tran: our infra team uses NFS for model artifacts which could be a factor, we need to move to a local cache for hot shards
06:04 Marcus Lee: agreed — local warm caches for weights/kv caches drastically reduce variance. we also recommend a small persistent memory cache for prefix KV where possible
06:15 Avery Chen: let's talk thresholds: Lyric's config currently fans out to 16 shards for some requests. what if we introduce a dynamic cap that drops to 6 during detected overload?
06:27 Gunnar Holt: that would help dramatically for p99 but could increase some per-request compute if we contract representation. i want numbers though
06:34 Marcus Lee: example from similar customer: static cap 8 dropped p99 from 480ms to 190ms in bursts, median stayed within 10ms; quality loss negligible with progressive merging
06:47 Marta Rivera: progressive merging sounds complex — is there an SDK helper?
06:52 Sofia Ortega: yes, Redwood ships a progressive-merge helper in the SDK that does top-k merging and score normalization, we can demo it in the pilot
07:03 Priya Nair: networks: you said multi-nic and AZ hops add 10-20ms sometimes; how do we detect when that anomalous route is used?
07:12 Connor Wu: trace correlation with BGP/route table events and node-level network counters; we can tag traces with 'cross-az' when source and dest AZ don't match. also check egress NAT gateway queues which can queue packets under load
07:28 Lee Tran: are there known kernel knobs for conntrack? we saw ephemeral conntrack exhaustion under fanout spikes
07:36 Marcus Lee: increase conntrack table sizes and tune timeouts for short-lived flows; but long term, move to connection pooling for internal gRPC to avoid creating thousands of ephemeral TCP flows per request
07:49 Priya Nair: connection pooling — is that supported in our current agent? we use the stock agent right now
07:54 Marcus Lee: yes, Redwood's runtime can enable keep-alive pooling between edge and kv backends; requires small config change and more stable sockets which reduce the hop penalty
08:05 Marta Rivera: i want to hear about backpressure — we saw a case where the runtime queued requests on the aggregator and that made p99 worse
08:14 Marcus Lee: right, when queuing is done at the wrong layer it amplifies tail. better to do early reject / shed at the ingress or apply token-bucket shaping per-tenant and signal upstream to slow down. queues are invisible amplification points
08:30 Priya Nair: so early shed + adaptive fanout + streaming optionally? that's a lot of moving parts for us to coordinate
08:36 Avery Chen: we usually roll these in phases: 1) telemetry and heatmap so we can pinpoint hotspots, 2) conservative config changes (conntrack, pooling, local cache), 3) fanout cap and progressive merge, 4) optional streaming experiments for specific flows.
08:53 Gunnar Holt: on instrumentation, we'll provide a kv heatmap csv and enable the extra trace propagation you mentioned
08:58 Marcus Lee: awesome. also wanted to call out an edge case: quantization can change tensor layout so the kernel selector might choose scalar fallback for some ops on older GPUs, that shows up as a 2-3x spike on certain ops
09:14 Sofia Ortega: yes and those are very hardware-specific — we should get a GPU profile from Lyric's on-prem nodes, list of GPU models and driver versions
09:24 Marta Rivera: we have 2x A5000 and some older V100 clones in the lab, not homogeneous
09:31 Marcus Lee: heterogeneous fleet increases variance. profiling will let us recommend per-model quantization profiles (some GPUs do better with 4-bit + int8 mix)
09:43 Priya Nair: about the pilot — we want to run a controlled burst test and a steady-state run, what are good signal windows?
09:51 Marcus Lee: run: 2 phases. burst test: ramp to target qps in 30s, hold 2m, measure p50/p95/p99; steady-state: 60m at target 2k qps, look for drift and rare spikes. include toggles for streaming, fanout cap, and conntrack tuning in each run
10:11 Lee Tran: who will own that run?
10:13 Priya Nair: we'll own infra side, Redwood runs the client harness and aggregates traces
10:18 Avery Chen: perfect. we also suggested a small on-prem bench to test mmap vs unpack and to validate quantized kernels with current drivers
10:27 Marcus Lee: one more note — when streaming is combined with prefix caching there's a subtle interaction: if the prefix is served from cache you don't pay the KV cost and streaming is always net positive; if prefix cache misses and we fanout, streaming may expose mid-request noise
10:47 Gunnar Holt: interesting, so perhaps condition streaming on prefix cache hit?
10:52 Sofia Ortega: that's exactly a pattern we've used: allow streaming only when prefixCacheHit==true or estimated fanout < threshold
11:03 Marta Rivera: are there any safety concerns with progressive merging? we want deterministic audits for outputs
11:10 Marcus Lee: progressive merging logs all intermediate merges and the merge provenance, so you can reconstitute final output deterministically given the same inputs. auditability preserved
11:22 Priya Nair: excellent. can you send an example log line?
11:26 Marcus Lee: yes we'll include sample provenance logs in the artifacts bundle
11:31 Avery Chen: quick recap: telemetry bundle, synthetic runs, config changes (conntrack/pooling/local cache), pilot schedule, and a SDK demo for progressive merge. anyone disagree?
11:41 Marta Rivera: no objections, sounds good
11:44 Gunnar Holt: yep
11:46 Lee Tran: we'll try to shift NFS hot artifacts into a local fast cache first week
11:50 Priya Nair: action items noted
11:54 Avery Chen: awesome. thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifact links and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
11:59 Marcus Lee: thanks all
12:02 Sofia Ortega: thanks
12:05 (call ends)
